source: Wang, Huang, Padmakumar, Lee (2026) Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance (q@Tail)
finding: Creativity benchmarks sit further in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution than standard benchmarks. A cheap diagnostic, q@Tail, measures task quality on the most novel 25% of an existing benchmark. Most creativity-promoting methods raise novelty but lower quality in the tail. Only min-p sampling raised tail quality.
numbers: 15 benchmarks, 26 open-weight models, 82 papers surveyed. Averaged over 4 models, 237-prompt creative mix. q@Tail vs vanilla 0.474: min-p 0.558 (+17.7%), convergent-divergent thinking 0.442 (-6.9%), temperature x1.5 0.441 (-7.0%), persona 0.421 (-11.2%), branch-solve-merge 0.408 (-13.9%), self-consistency 0.384 (-19.0%), meta-prompting 0.320 (-32.5%), temperature x2.0 0.212 (-55.3%), CRPO-SFT 0.130, CRPO-DPO 0.098. Min-p lowered overall novelty 16.3% and novelty at peak 44.2%. CoT q@Tail 0.539, Claude Opus 4.6 High 0.610. Kendall tau with LM Arena creative-writing rank: 0.37 (p=0.029) for most-tail benchmark vs 0.16 (n.s.) for Alpaca. Tail bins tau +0.33 vs +0.06 to +0.15 for peak bins.
quote: Most methods increase output novelty without consistently improving quality in the tail
limits: Tailness uses Pile n-gram statistics, so it measures surface rarity, not conceptual novelty. Quality scored by a reward model (Skywork-Reward-V2-8B) on three datasets. Arena creative ranking is strongly coupled with general capability. Average over 4 models only. Table values were read from flattened PDF text and matched to methods by column order, checked against the paper's own text (min-p +17.7%, CoT 0.539).
agent_relevance: Any creative mode we add must be scored on quality inside the novel region, not on novelty alone. Report quality-at-tail next to novelty. Wrapper methods (persona, branch-solve-merge, self-consistency, meta-prompting) did worse than the plain model on this measure.

source: Wadhwa et al. (2026) Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
finding: A set-level RL objective (each idea's quality weighted by its distance from earlier ideas in the same set) lifts creative utility of an 8B model above frontier closed models on a contamination-free ideation test. Quality-only set RL collapses the set onto one idea.
numbers: Test set 1,740 instances, 16 domains. Creative utility (CU, beta=0.9): base 0.03, SFT 0.21, proposed (no think) 0.64, proposed (think) 0.51, DARLING 0.52, Claude Opus 4.8 0.38, GPT-6 Astra 0.28. Impact-only RL: win rate 43% but mean distance fell to 0.38. Proposed distance 0.88 vs DARLING 0.67. Without SFT: grounding 0.19 vs 0.81.
limits: Requires training, so it is not directly usable in our scaffold-only agent. Quality is an LLM impact judge; the CU metric is the authors' own. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Gives the design target for an open mode: reward the set, not the single idea. Without training we can only imitate it by scoring each new idea by distance to earlier ones and rejecting near copies.

source: Wadhwa et al. (2026) Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas (set prompting vs independent sampling)
finding: Asking a general model for a set of K=3 ideas in one response (instead of 3 independent samples) raises idea distance sharply but lowers quality for closed models. Net utility barely changes.
numbers: Distance 0.24-0.53 (sampled) to 0.79-0.86 (set prompt). Claude Opus 4.8: distance 0.24 to 0.80, win rate 0.33 to 0.21, CU 0.34 to 0.38. Trained model: win rate 0.50 and distance 0.88.
limits: One test set, one judge family. Per-model standard deviations not read.
agent_relevance: Set-level prompting is a cheap diversity lever (about 3x distance) but costs about a third of idea quality. Use it for the explore step, then filter and refine.

source: Wadhwa et al. (2026) Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas (human and execution checks)
finding: Small human study: the trained 8B model's portfolios were about as promising and as unique as Claude Opus 4.8's. A coding agent that executed 132 ideas found no quality loss against Opus.
numbers: 4 annotators, 60 instances (15 papers each). Promising ideas per portfolio: proposed 2.17, Opus 2.20, Qwen3-8B 1.52. Unique ideas: 2.83, 2.72, 2.52. Execution: 132 ideas, 15 instances (14 for think variant), success@k rose with k.
limits: Very small human panel and 15 execution instances. No significance claim against Opus; only as good as.
agent_relevance: Treat set-diversity gains as unproven on correctness until execution checks are larger.

source: Beaty et al. (2026) AGC-Bench: Measuring Artificial General Creativity
finding: Across 83 LLMs and 78 datasets, one general creativity factor explains most of the variance. It correlates with reasoning and knowledge but stays separable. This implies that model-level differences in creativity type are small compared with one overall level.
numbers: 497 benchmarks found, 3,101 papers screened, 78 datasets in first release. C factor explains 81.5% of variance across six text domains (omega 0.96); holds after partialling out fluid reasoning (0.91). AGC composite vs letter-string analogy rho +0.55 (n=82). Parameters vs composite rho +0.69 (42 open models), +0.37 with active parameters. Composite predicts model agreement with human ratings on an independent 1,862-response corpus: r +0.66 (n=74). AGC-Judge (Qwen3-30B-A3B LoRA on 48,299 JRT-corrected ratings): rho 0.94 on held-out items, 0.83 on three held-out benchmarks.
limits: Scores are relative to the tested cohort. Mostly English text. Judges are three frontier LLMs, so shared biases remain. It does not test Boden's three types.
agent_relevance: Backbone choice may matter more than mode choice. A cheap single judge fine-tuned on calibrated ratings is feasible but needs training; we can borrow the idea of judge-leniency calibration (JRT) with a panel.

source: Beaty et al. (2026) AGC-Bench (style-flip paraphrase probe of the judge)
finding: To test whether the judge rewards style instead of ideas, the authors paraphrased 50 answers keeping every idea but changing register (humans rewritten to polished LLM style, LLMs to casual style). Scores barely moved.
numbers: 50 cells (5 humans + 5 LLMs per task). Mean score change: polish +0.40 (d=0.29), humanize +0.52 (d=0.15) on a 10-50 scale. Paraphraser: Grok-4.1-fast.
quote: holding the underlying idea constant and swapping stylistic register barely shifts AGC-Judge
limits: Only 50 cells, one paraphraser, one judge. This tests register, not deep reordering of concepts, and cannot rule out all style effects (authors say so). Does not test whether truly novel concepts are detected.
agent_relevance: First direct paraphrase-stability number for an LLM creativity judge. Run the same style-flip check on our novelty judge before trusting it.

source: Beaty et al. (2026) AGC-Bench (judge vs human gold)
finding: AGC-Judge agrees more with an existing LLM judge than with human creativity ratings. Residual self-preference for LLM text remains.
numbers: n=718. Spearman 0.65 vs human creativity gold, 0.80 vs LLM-judge gold; Williams test t=-7.98 (Spearman), p<0.0001. On human-written stories AGC-Judge aligned equally with human and LLM gold (both about +0.74). Fairness-aware composite vs human-panel composite rho +0.60 (LLM-only +0.76, human-only +0.58).
limits: Human panel size not read in detail. Single corpus.
agent_relevance: Do not read an LLM-judged novelty gain as human-visible novelty. Keep a small human spot check in any evaluation of the open mode.

source: Lu, Wang, Li, Jiang, Khudanpur, Jiang, Khashabi (2025) Benchmarking Language Model Creativity: A Case Study on Code Generation (Denial Prompting, Table 3)
finding: Rule dropping by forbidding the previous technique steadily destroys correctness. Divergence rises while convergent quality falls to zero by state 4-5. GPT-4 is the only model that keeps going.
numbers: 199 Codeforces problems, 30 correct human solutions each (5.9K), 2.2K test examples. GPT-4 by constraint state t=0..5: pass@1 16.1, 11.6, 7.1, 5.2, 2.3, 2.1 (%); constraint following 100, 75.4, 46.0, 33.0, 26.1, 14.4; convergent creative 16.2, 8.1, 3.6, 1.6, 0.0, 0.0; divergent creative 4.5, 11.9, 11.5, 12.4, 13.2, 15.3; NeoGauge 1.0, 1.4, 0.9, 0.5, 0, 0. Claude-3 and Llama3-70B fell to 0 within two states after state 0. Humans also lose convergent score with t.
quote: unlike the convergent score, which typically decreases as t increases, the divergent score of GPT-4 continually rises
limits: Task is competitive programming with unit tests; the dropped rule is a technique ban, not a change to the problem itself. Divergence needs 30 human solutions as a reference. Low pass@1 at state 0 (16.1%) limits all numbers. Authors argue problems may not be infeasible at high t, not proven. Column-to-value mapping of Table 3 read from flattened text.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 for checkable tasks: every dropped or added rule should be followed by an executable check (tests plus constraint adherence). Plan a cap of about 2-3 rule changes before correctness collapses.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Denial Prompting (validity checks: technique detection and constraint following)
finding: The paper's cheap check that a new rule is both valid and obeyed: run unit tests for correctness, then detect the atomic techniques used and test them against the forbidden set. GPT-4 serves as the technique detector.
numbers: GPT-4 reached 94% technique-detection recall against a human programmer in a pilot. Reasoning strategies were compared; only MCTS raised divergent creativity after step 2 (see c20 in evidence_c).
limits: Pilot size for the 94% recall was not stated in the passage read. Detector and generator are the same model family, so shared blind spots are possible. Needs a code domain; no equivalent for prose.
agent_relevance: Pattern to copy: validity of a rule change = (a) original correctness test still passes, (b) forbidden element absent, checked by a separate detector. For non-code tasks use a second model call as detector plus a human-written spot test.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Is Imagination Derived from Hallucination? Whiteboard benchmark
finding: Scores invention that the prompt licenses (imagination) and invention that crosses the support boundary (hallucination) on the same generation, with deterministic scoring and no LLM judge. Across 79 models, imagination and destructive hallucination are negatively coupled, not positively.
numbers: 1,660-prompt bank; 80-item anchor set; 79 LLMs from 18 providers; 6,229 valid generations. 23 of 189 cells survive triple FDR, 22 negative. All 55 eligible items negative, 54 significant, median rho -0.63. Aggregate coupling about -0.414 after length and date controls, -0.093 after capability control. Validation: 13,280 blind human judgments; output-level tracking 0.72 (imagination) and 0.69 (hallucination), model level 0.56 and 0.67. Annotators licensed unsupported content at 18.7-22.8% across ten subtypes.
quote: imagination to be the antidote to hallucination, not its byproduct
limits: Correlational. One response per item. Capability proxy removes most of the aggregate coupling. Not about Boden modes. Item bank not mapped to rule changes.
agent_relevance: Supports separating licensed novelty from unlicensed invention in the rule-drop step: a new rule is valid only if the task or user licenses it. About one fifth of unsupported content passes as licensed for humans, so add a check against the original goal.

source: Lingo and Chhajer (2026) Dynamic Context Evolution for Scalable Synthetic Data Generation
finding: Prompting repeatedly without memory causes cross-batch mode collapse. A persistent memory that rejects near duplicates stops it; a self-rated how-obvious-is-this filter (verbalized tail sampling) and prompt evolution add breadth.
numbers: 200 batches, packaging domain, 2-3 seeds, two model families (gpt-5-mini, claude-haiku-4-5). Collapse (near-duplicates of first 50 batches at cosine 0.85): naive 5.6 +/- 2.0%, any method with dedup 0.0 +/- 0.0%. In the exam-question domain 34% of late questions repeated early ones; packaging 4%. Naive batch novelty fell from 1.0 to about 0.20 within 60 batches and cluster count plateaued after batch 60. HDBSCAN clusters: DCE 17-18 vs naive 2-17, dedup-only 9. EDV retention: DCE 23.6 +/- 3.5% vs dedup-only 26.1% (single seed); DCE advantage p=0.50 Wilcoxon, not significant.
quote: cross-batch mode collapse: the progressive loss of output diversity when a language model is prompted repeatedly without access to its prior generations
limits: Cost per accepted idea (tokens) is not reported in the passages read. Embedding choice changes top ranks (OpenAI vs MiniLM embeddings swap the top two). 2-3 seeds. Domain is synthetic data, not creative problem solving. Authors call the EDV difference directional only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the yield plateau: independent batches saturate about batch 60. Add a persistent semantic memory of accepted ideas inside the open mode and stop when new clusters stop appearing.

source: Lingo and Chhajer (2026) Dynamic Context Evolution (verbalized tail filter vs dedup; explore-then-fill schedule)
finding: The verbalized-probability filter and the duplicate filter act on almost non-overlapping idea sets. The campaign used 40% broad exploration then 60% gap filling, but never compared this with a constant mix.
numbers: Of 852 ideas the tail filter would reject (self-rated probability <= 0.10), 826 (96.9%) were semantically novel and would pass dedup; dedup caught only 30 ideas (3.0%). Self-rated probability vs distance from centroid: Spearman -0.065, p=0.04 (weak). Gap-targeting strategy degraded over time: 90.8% acceptance, lowest mean EDV (0.265), 707 unique labels for 950 ideas.
limits: Weak calibration of self-rated obviousness (rho about -0.07). The tail filter's value on idea quality is untested here. No ablation of the 40/60 schedule, so gap 8 stays open for the schedule question.
agent_relevance: Verbalized obviousness is a cheap but weak filter; keep a real duplicate filter as the main guard. Test the explore-then-refine split ourselves against a constant mix.

source: Min Sen, Chun et al. (2026) Automated Creativity Evaluation of Language Models Across Open-Ended Tasks
finding: Step-level and solution-level semantic entropy (clusters of meaning, n=10 samples per step) is a reference-free measure of divergent exploration. It beat surface diversity metrics on agreement with human preferences and tracked an LLM novelty judge that had itself been checked against humans.
numbers: Domains: MacGyver, HypoGen, BookMIA. SE agreement with human preference rho 0.56, higher than cosine similarity, Self-BLEU, Distinct-n. LLM novelty judge vs 5-annotator majority on 30 MacGyver solutions: Spearman 0.80. SE and convergent-quality metrics only weakly correlated. Divergent creativity did not scale with model size or recency while convergent did. Retrieval-based multi-agent judge: accuracy comparable to single human annotators on 50 MacGyver and 50 BookMIA solutions, over 60% cheaper.
limits: Only 30 human-ranked pairs for novelty, annotators had only moderate agreement. Entailment model chosen on 55 pairs. Semantic entropy measures spread of meaning, which can be conceptual or merely surface-level; no paraphrase test.
agent_relevance: Semantic entropy over clustered meanings is a cheap, judge-free diversity signal usable as a stop rule. It is not a validated measure of conceptual novelty.

source: Chang (2025) Magellan: Guided MCTS for Latent Space Exploration and Novelty Generation
finding: A guided search (MCTS with a semantic compass and a novelty-aware value) beat ReAct, ToT and CoT in LLM-judged scientific ideas on a tiny backbone. Evidence is weak: independent author, one 1.7B model, LLM judge only.
numbers: Backbone Qwen3-1.7B for all methods; judge DeepSeek-V3.1-Think. Overall score 8.94 with 92.0% win rate; vs AI Scientist and SciPip 90.0% win; removing novelty term cut win rate to 2.0%. MCTS averaged 3 iterations (cap 30). ToT input-to-output token ratio 1.73:1. Performance rose strongly with backbone size; Qwen-0.6B failed.
limits: No equal-token comparison in the passages read; the paper admits higher cost than CoT. Single small backbone, no second backbone, no checkable task, no human panel. Not a Boden-mode test.
agent_relevance: Does NOT close gap 1. It shows that a search wrapper (not a named Boden mode) can beat ToT on a small model under an LLM judge; treat as low confidence.

source: Espirito Santo, Wiggins, Cardoso (2024) Towards a Formal Creativity Theory (reading of Boden and Wiggins definitions)
finding: Quotes Wiggins (2019) as describing Boden's transformational creativity as transforming the rule set that defines a conceptual space. Their own formal version: a learner changes hypothesis after seeing an artefact (transformativeness). They prove novelty is neither necessary nor sufficient for transformation in general, but is necessary for set-driven agents that ignore order and repetition.
numbers: Definition 17 (Transformativeness): artefact a is transformative in situation s iff M(sigma) differs from M(sigma + a). Theorem on novelty: not necessary, not sufficient over sequences; necessary for order-blind set-driven agents.
limits: Secondary for Boden, but Wiggins is a coauthor. Theory only, no data. Boden 2004 and Wiggins 2006 themselves were NOT opened.
agent_relevance: A prompt that forbids a technique changes the output filter, not the generator's internal hypothesis. Under this definition a transformation is observed only if the model's own way of generating changes after the new input. Track whether outputs change in kind (new method class), not just in surface.

source: Schapiro, Black, Varshney (2025) Transformational Creativity in Science: A Graphical Theory
finding: Conceptual spaces are DAGs of constraints. Axioms are sink nodes; rules depend on other nodes. Modifying an axiom has the greatest transformative potential, because it has the most dependents.
numbers: Theorem 4: the node with greatest transformative potential must be an axiom. Examples: removal of the parallel postulate (Euclid to non-Euclidean), Copernican and Kepler shifts, special relativity.
limits: Short paper, no empirical test on LLMs. Formal definition applies to scientific spaces; mapping to code or ideation tasks is our inference.
agent_relevance: Inference for our design: a prompt-level rule drop such as banning one technique edits a leaf rule with few dependents, so it gives low transformative potential. Real transformation needs the model to find and revise an axiom (a base assumption of the task) and re-derive consequences. A candidate operator: list task assumptions, rank by dependents, drop one, re-derive, then check.

source: arXiv title/abstract searches run this session for independent replication or follow-up of Universe of Thoughts
finding: No independent replication or extension of Universe of Thoughts was found. Searches for transformational creativity, exploratory creativity, Boden creativity language models and Denial Prompting returned UoT as the only paper using Boden-typed operators for reasoning, beside OMEGA, KOMBINE and CreativeBench. Semantic Scholar showed no citing papers for arXiv 2511.20471.
numbers: arXiv abstract search 'transformational creativity': 50 results, only UoT is a Boden-typed LLM reasoning paper. 'Universe of Thoughts' exact: 1 matching title (24 results total, the rest astronomy). Semantic Scholar citations endpoint returned an empty list.
limits: Negative search result. arXiv search was AND-based and rate-limited; web search quota ran out; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited, so citation lists may be incomplete or not yet indexed. UoT latest version dated 6 Oct 2026, so replication time was short.
agent_relevance: Treat all Boden-typed LLM results as single-source. Plan our own replication on a second backbone and judge family before trusting mode choices.

source: arXiv and web search for TwistBench (unread item from critique)
finding: TwistBench could not be located. arXiv returned no results and a web search found no paper with that name. Nearest items were Creativity Benchmark (2509.09702), CreativityPrism (2510.20091), AGC-Bench (2607.01152) and the long-tail paper (2610.12998).
limits: May be a misspelt name or an unindexed paper. Evidence is the absence of a hit.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 part on TwistBench stays open. Do not cite it.

source: Boden (1998) Creativity and artificial intelligence, Artificial Intelligence 103; Wiggins (2006) papers (access attempts)
finding: Primary texts could not be opened: Elsevier and ACM pages returned 403 or a bare redirect, and the Goldsmiths PDF paths returned 404. Boden and Wiggins definitions here therefore come from d15 and d16 (opened) plus earlier second-hand lines.
numbers: Access attempts: sciencedirect 403, doi redirect page empty, dl.acm.org 403, doc.gold.ac.uk KBS06 and NGC06 404.
limits: Gap 7 stays only partly closed: definitions seen through Wiggins (2019, quoted by Espirito Santo et al. 2024) and Schapiro et al. 2025 who cite Boden 1992 enabling constraints. No verbatim Boden 2004 text.
agent_relevance: Before building a rule-change operator on the claim that Boden says so, someone with library access should check Boden 2004 ch. 4 and the Wiggins 2006 section on meta-level search.
